name: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7
lead: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Pal-GQPR, also sold as Rigin) is a synthetic peptide of glycine, glutamine, proline and arginine attached to palmitic acid, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin cosmetics. It is applied as a serum or cream ingredient with the aim of calming skin inflammation and supporting the collagen and basement-membrane structure so skin looks smoother and firmer.[2] It is described as an anti-inflammatory signal peptide and is the second peptide in Sederma's Matrixyl 3000 complex, alongside palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[2][1]

Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, reports that it decreases IL-6 secretion in laboratory models and promotes laminin and collagen VII production.[2] Peptides in general are widely used in sensitive-skin products: an analysis of 88 facial cosmetics found peptides in 17 percent, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 among them, while noting that much of the supporting data sits in patents and supplier brochures rather than randomized placebo-controlled studies.[3]

Published human efficacy data specific to this peptide alone are limited. Studies of eye creams and serums have tested it in combination with other actives, and a 2026 study imaged how the Matrixyl 3000 peptides move into the outer skin layer.[5][9]

angle.text: The peptide is used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products to soften the look of fine lines and redness. Reported effects in cells and in multi-ingredient product studies are the basis for these claims.

paras: The palmitoyl group, a 16-carbon fatty acid chain on the glycine end, raises lipophilicity to aid passage through the stratum corneum.[2] The same strategy is used for related cosmetic peptides: Wikipedia describes palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Matrixyl), launched by Sederma in 2000, as a five-amino-acid peptide attached to a 16-carbon fatty chain meant to help it cross the skin's lipid layers.[7] Grokipedia says palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 was introduced in the early 2000s as part of Matrixyl 3000 and appears in products from brands such as The Ordinary and Paula's Choice.[2]

It appears in multi-peptide formulations; a US drug-label listing for a stretch-mark cream names it alongside tripeptide-1, hexapeptide-9, acetyl tetrapeptide-9, palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 and acetyl hexapeptide-8.[6]

Sederma, the French cosmetic ingredient company, launched Matrixyl (palmitoyl pentapeptide-4) in 2000, and Grokipedia reports that palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 came in the early 2000s as part of the Matrixyl 3000 complex, paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[7][2] Palmitoylated peptides became a common design for cosmetic peptides because the fatty-acid chain is intended to carry the peptide into the outer skin.[7][2] It is often sold under the name Rigin and appears on ingredient lists of anti-ageing and sensitive-skin serums.[2]

Reported laboratory effects include lowering IL-6 secretion after stressors such as UVB, and promoting basement membrane proteins such as laminin IV and V and collagen VII.[2] A 2015 study of dermal extracellular matrix and the epidermal-dermal junction used mass-spectrometric imaging, in vivo reflectance confocal microscopy, echography and histology to examine age-related changes and then tested a blend of palmitoyl oligopeptide and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7; it found that selected matrix proteins were less abundant in aged skin explants than in young ones.[4]
A 2026 knowledge-graph and docking study screened peptide ingredients for type III collagen mechanisms in cosmetics.[8]

A 2026 study used time-of-flight and orbital-trapping secondary ion mass spectrometry to track cosmetic actives into the stratum corneum in three healthy female volunteers. Serums containing Matrixyl 3000 were applied for 0.5, 2 and 5 hours, and both peptides, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, were detected in stratum corneum layers with signal decreasing with depth.[5]

Wikipedia and ingredient references describe peptides as signal molecules in anti-wrinkle products, and a review of sensitive-skin cosmetics found three of seven peptides in the products analysed worked by a neurotransmitter-inhibiting mechanism and three were signal peptides; only five had evidence supporting use in sensitive skin and only one clinical study included volunteers with sensitive skin.[3][7]

A 12-week clinical trial of a multi-component anti-aging eye cream containing yeast/rice fermentation filtrate, N-acetylneuraminic acid, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 assessed hydration (Corneometer), elasticity (Cutometer), photographs (VISIA) and collagen density (ultrasound), with dermatologists and participants rating efficacy at baseline and weeks 4, 8 and 12. The authors reported improvements in skin hydration (28.12 percent), elasticity (18.81 percent) and collagen production (54.99 percent), and fibroblast experiments showed increased collagen and elastin synthesis; because the cream contained several actives, effects cannot be assigned to one ingredient.[9] No trial of this peptide alone was found.

Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is named on labels alongside palmitoyl tripeptide-1.[2][3] An analysis of 88 facial cosmetics found peptides in 17 percent of them, palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 among them, and also noted that much of the supporting evidence for peptides in sensitive-skin products rests on in vitro or manufacturer studies.[3] As a cosmetic ingredient it is sold over the counter in serums, creams and eye products, and some products list it in combination with several other peptides rather than on its own.[6][9]

card.summary: The anti-inflammatory peptide half of Matrixyl 3000; present in many serums, with little isolated human data.
card.note: Mechanism claims come largely from lab data and an AI-generated reference.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 is a lab-made peptide with a fatty acid tail, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. It is paired with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 in Matrixyl 3000.

Its effects in people have mostly been studied inside multi-ingredient products, not on its own.
quick.mechanism: In lab models it is reported to reduce inflammatory IL-6 release and to support skin matrix proteins.
quick.risks: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient; labels advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. No ingredient-specific safety data were found.
